clue.text: This band is in first class order

definitions.text: This band is in first class order

parts.words: This band is in first class order
parts.note: a band worn below the knee that also names the most senior English order of chivalry

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that their band of musicians is in top-notch shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'order' look musical or tidy, but the band is a strip of material and the order is the Order of the Garter, England's highest order of knighthood.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter is an elastic band holding up a stocking, and it gives its name to Britain's premier chivalric order.

clue.text: Not necessarily designed for the fuller figure

definitions.text: Not necessarily designed for the fuller figure

parts.words: Not necessarily designed for the fuller figure
parts.note: a heavy overcoat whose size word refers to warmth and length, not the wearer's girth

explanation.surface: A garment not cut for the larger body shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fuller figure' suggests a large person, but the 'great' in the name refers to the heavy cloth, not to the wearer.
explanation.definitionFit: A greatcoat is a long heavy overcoat, typically military, with nothing to do with the size of its owner.

clue.text: Ruddy girl wasn't on a hunger strike

parts.note: Rose is a girl's name
someone not refusing food simply took meals

explanation.surface: A rosy-cheeked girl who has clearly not been starving herself.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean rosy or pink-tinted.

clue.text: What to expect of a regular waster

definitions.text: What to expect of a regular waster

parts.words: What to expect of a regular waster
parts.note: waster read as something that wastes the body away, so regular wasting leaves one gaunt

explanation.surface: What becomes of a habitual idler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waster' suggests a layabout, but here it is someone who keeps wasting away, growing thinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Wasting away leaves the body extremely thin and gaunt.

clue.text: A Scotland Yard examination, looking for gold?

parts.note: CID, the Criminal Investigation Department, is the detective branch at Scotland Yard
an examination is a test

explanation.surface: Detectives from London's police headquarters examine a scene, perhaps hunting stolen gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the London Metropolitan Police headquarters. The definition is fair because nitric acid was used to check whether metal was genuine gold, which is where the phrase comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Assayers dropped nitric acid on metal to tell real gold from base metal; the phrase now means any decisive trial.

clue.text: Its charms are varied

indicators.note: letters that are varied are changed in their order, rearranging the two words before

explanation.surface: A remark that the festive season's delights come in many kinds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are varied' rearranges ITS CHARMS; the whole clue also describes the festive season, so it doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The December festival offers many different pleasures, from presents to carols.

clue.text: Fate of Aunt Ada of Cold Comfort Farm

definitions.text: Aunt Ada of Cold Comfort Farm

explanation.surface: A literary question about what became of a character in a comic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stella Gibbons's 1932 comic novel Cold Comfort Farm, the matriarch Aunt Ada has this surname and once 'saw something nasty in the woodshed'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means destiny, especially a grim one, and it is the surname of the old matriarch in Gibbons's novel.

clue.text: Record the singular weight of this witticism

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
I, the first person singular, is the singular pronoun
a gram is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A request to log the exact heaviness of a clever saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: an EP disc. 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short, pointed, witty saying.

clue.text: Can a slacker become thus fuddled?

definitions.text: Can a slacker become thus fuddled?

parts.words: Can a slacker become thus fuddled?
parts.note: a slack rope can be pulled taut, and the same word means drunk

explanation.surface: Asking whether an idler might end up drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slacker' looks like a lazy person, but it is something slacker, like a rope, which can become taut; the word is also slang for drunk, or fuddled.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means taut, the opposite of slack, and is also slang for drunk.

clue.text: Light troubling the eye.

explanation.surface: Bright light causing discomfort to someone's vision.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the Gospel saying about the beam in your own eye, a plank of wood that troubles it more than the mote in another's.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray of light, and the timber in the Sermon on the Mount that a hypocrite overlooks in their own eye.

clue.text: Shuffle — a cut — see, Diamonds, my boy!

indicators.note: shuffling cards mixes them, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A card player calls out shuffle, cut and look to a young son, with diamonds as trumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuffle' and 'cut' look like card-table words, but 'Shuffle' scrambles A CUT SEE. The definition points to Trollope's novel The Eustace Diamonds: the boy's name is the one that goes before 'Diamonds'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eustace is a boy's first name, and the Trollope title The Eustace Diamonds pairs it with the gems.

clue.text: Something protective to go in for, in a way

indicators.note: done in a way means done after a fashion, so the letters are put into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to take up some protective pursuit, after a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' looks like a hedge, but it is the anagram signal on GO IN FOR; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A covering laid over the top of a house shields it from rain and weather.

clue.text: Mrs Siddons according to Reynolds

parts.note: the title of Joshua Reynolds's famous portrait of the actress Sarah Siddons names the role he painted her in

explanation.surface: How a painter saw a celebrated Georgian actress.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Siddons was the great tragic actress of 18th-century London; Reynolds painted her as Melpomene, the inspiring goddess of tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Reynolds's portrait is titled Mrs Siddons as the goddess of tragedy, Melpomene, so that is what he made of her.

clue.text: Determination won't improve one's bearing

explanation.surface: Sheer willpower will not make anyone's posture any better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' looks like posture, but it is a machine bearing: sand or dust in one makes it wear and seize.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit means pluck and resolve, and it is also abrasive sand that damages moving machine parts.

clue.text: Result of putting an extra bit on, perhaps

definitions.text: Result of putting an extra bit on, perhaps

indicators.note: the outcome of putting, or placing, these letters differently is a new arrangement of them

explanation.surface: A remark about what happens when a little extra is added to the price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Result of putting' rearranges EXTRA BIT ON; 'an' and 'perhaps' are links. The whole clue also describes an inflated price.
explanation.definitionFit: Charging an extra amount on top makes a price excessive.

clue.text: The classic matricide

parts.note: the Greek hero who killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father Agamemnon

explanation.surface: The best-known mother-killer of ancient legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classic' means from Greek classical literature, not merely typical.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aeschylus and Sophocles, Agamemnon's son slays his mother Clytemnestra, making him the archetypal killer of a parent.

clue.text: What the babes did with fine timber?

explanation.surface: Asking what the children in the story did with some good-quality wood.
explanation.walkthrough: In the old tale the Babes in the Wood were abandoned in a forest, so they 'sat in wood'; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as three words it describes the children of the tale; as one it is a lustrous hardwood used in fine furniture.

clue.text: Make the most of it; you'll get no more

explanation.surface: Advice to enjoy what you have, since there is nothing more coming.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the greatest amount possible, and that upper limit is the point beyond which nothing more is given.

clue.text: Gunman brought to book in France

definitions.text: Gunman brought to book in France

parts.words: Gunman brought to book in France
parts.note: an armed soldier made famous in a French novel by Dumas rather than one arrested

explanation.surface: An armed criminal finally caught by the French police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought to book' suggests arrest, but it means written into a book: Dumas's The Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: A musketeer was a soldier armed with a musket, and Dumas made the musket-bearing guards famous.

clue.text: An outsider in the matter of clothes

definitions.text: An outsider in the matter of clothes

parts.words: An outsider in the matter of clothes
parts.note: an outsider here is a garment worn on the outside, over all the other layers

explanation.surface: Someone who does not fit in when it comes to fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outsider' suggests a misfit, but it means the outermost layer of clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcoat goes on over everything else, so it is literally the outer garment.

clue.text: If a boy, he probably grew up brave

definitions.text: If a boy, he probably grew up brave

parts.words: If a boy, he probably grew up brave
parts.note: a North American Indigenous infant, a boy of whom would become a warrior, called a brave

explanation.surface: A remark about a boy who grew up to be courageous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brave' looks like an adjective, but it is the old noun for a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, borrowed from Algonquian, means a Native American baby or the carrier it rides in.

clue.text: Fiddling difficulties?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether petty cheating leads to trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddling' suggests cheating, but here it is scraping a bow across a violin.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraping is the rough sawing of an amateur violinist, and awkward predicaments are also called this.

clue.text: Smallness of France's SW resort city

parts.note: Pau is a resort town in south-west France at the foot of the Pyrenees
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dismissive comment on how small a city in south-western France is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means scarcity or a small amount of something.

clue.text: Drinks to-night

parts.note: drinks that, joined to the word night, make the name for a bedtime tipple

explanation.surface: An invitation for drinks this evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to-night' reads as this evening, but it means 'to go with night': put NIGHT in front and you get nightcaps, drinks taken before bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightcaps are drinks before bed; the clue wants the word that completes them after night.

clue.text: His heart attacks don't prove fatal

definitions.text: His heart attacks don't prove fatal

parts.words: His heart attacks don't prove fatal
parts.note: the god of love shoots arrows at hearts, making people fall in love rather than die

explanation.surface: Someone whose cardiac episodes never kill him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart attacks' suggests a medical crisis, but it means his arrows aimed at hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of love wounds hearts with his arrows to make people fall in love.

clue.text: No fit state — such foolishness

explanation.surface: Someone is in no condition to behave, and that is how silly they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such' is a link. Inept means unfit, so the first definition is the condition of being unfit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the noun of inept, so it is both the condition of being unsuitable and plain clumsy folly.

clue.text: Design gent finds noisy

explanation.surface: A man discovers that a scheme is rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition says this word, when it finds 'gent' after it, makes PLANGENT, meaning loud and resonant.
explanation.definitionFit: A design is a scheme or layout; joined to 'gent' it gives a word for resounding.

clue.text: Singer eager to turn up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means reading the word from the bottom upwards, so backwards

parts.note: avid means eager

explanation.surface: A vocalist keen to make an appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn up' looks like arriving, but it reverses AVID in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A diva is a celebrated female opera singer.

clue.text: With this one is never out of condition

definitions.text: With this one is never out of condition

parts.words: With this one is never out of condition
parts.note: condition here is a stipulation in a contract rather than physical fitness

explanation.surface: A fitness regime that keeps you permanently in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of condition' suggests unfit, but a proviso is itself a condition, so with one you always have a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A proviso is a clause in an agreement making it subject to a stipulation.

clue.text: Undue desire for caviare, perhaps.

indicators.note: perhaps says the word that follows is only one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: A greedy craving for the luxury of sturgeon roe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges CAVIARE, an old spelling of caviar.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed is an excessive desire for wealth or possessions.

clue.text: Though dogged in principle, they have catlike characteristics

definitions.text: Though dogged in principle, they have catlike characteristics

parts.words: Though dogged in principle, they have catlike characteristics
parts.note: stubborn people who, like a cat with nine lives, take a great deal of killing

explanation.surface: Stubborn people who nonetheless behave like cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dogged' and 'catlike' set dog against cat; the catlike trait is being hard to kill, as a cat is said to have nine lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardliners who refuse to give up a cause are said to resist change to the last.

clue.text: One reluctant to "have a go"?

parts.note: someone who prefers remaining to leaving, read as one unwilling to depart

explanation.surface: A timid person unwilling to try something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have a go' sounds like making an attempt, but it is read as going away; a horse with stamina for long races is also called this.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who remains rather than leaving; also a horse or runner with staying power.
